title: Roadmaps and Horizons

know: The balanced roadmap of Build What Matters: innovation, iteration and operation, each with a deliberate share.
Outcome-based roadmap items and horizons of decreasing certainty.
What a roadmap commits to and to whom.
believe: A roadmap is a statement of intended outcomes in order, and treating it as a delivery contract with dates makes it false.
can_do: Classify roadmap items into innovation, iteration and operation and judge the balance.
Rewrite a dated feature list as a roadmap with horizons.
Say how far ahead a roadmap can honestly look for a given organization.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given a roadmap of dated features, the reader rewrites three items as outcomes at the right horizon and says what the roadmap may promise a customer.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A roadmap reads: 'Q1 offline mode; Q2 route optimization v2; Q3 customer portal redesign; Q4 AI dispatch.' Using only this chapter: what is wrong with it as a commitment, and how would the Q3 and Q4 items be stated?
acceptance_criteria.expected: It commits to solutions and dates a year out; near items can be solutions with dates, later ones should be outcomes with decreasing precision (for example 'customers can see and change their own appointments'), promised as direction and not as delivery dates.

acceptance_criteria.statement: The chapter says what AI changes about roadmap horizons with labeled claims.
Concepts taken from a named source name the book and the concept; rules of thumb are presented as that author's rule of thumb; anything applied beyond the source is marked as the author's extension.
Each pattern in the chapter names its user and an outcome measure by which a reader could tell that it worked.

thesis.question: What should a roadmap commit to, and how far ahead can it honestly look?
thesis.claim: A roadmap should commit to outcomes in an order, with a stated share of capacity for each of innovation, iteration and operation; it can honestly name solutions and dates only as far ahead as one learning cycle of the organization, the near horizon, and beyond that it can name only the problems, with decreasing precision; a roadmap that names features and dates a year out is a promise the organization cannot know it will keep.
thesis.disputed_by: The view of sales, customers and boards that a roadmap is a commitment to deliver named features on dates, and that anything less is evasion.
thesis.so_what: A leader publishes one roadmap with stated horizons, gives customers direction and near-term dates only, and defends a deliberate share of capacity for operation and iteration.
thesis.how_why: What is known about a solution falls quickly with distance in time, while what is known about the customer's problem holds; so the honest content of a distant item is the problem. Without a stated balance, urgent operational and customer-specific work takes the whole roadmap.

supporting_claims.claim: A roadmap of dated features can be delivered in full and still fail, because it states solutions and says nothing about what changes for customers.
A roadmap exists to connect near-term work to the strategy and the vision, so its items are outcomes in an order, and a feature is one candidate solution to an outcome.
A roadmap needs a stated share of capacity for each of innovation, iteration and operation, decided before any item is ranked, or urgent and customer-specific work takes all of it.
Solutions and dates can be named honestly only within one learning cycle of the organization; beyond it the roadmap can name outcomes and then only problems, with decreasing precision.
One roadmap with stated horizons tells customers, sales and the board what each horizon promises: dates near, direction far.
The demand for dated features a year out is answered by what can truthfully be planned on, and a date kept that far ahead is kept by not learning.

role.contribution: Lays the strategy out in time and fixes what each horizon may promise.

additional_patterns.applies_to: what-a-roadmap-is-for, the-balanced-roadmap, the-learning-cycle, one-roadmap-stated-horizons: the form of an item before the share among items, both before how far ahead items can be named, and the horizons before what each promises

flow.rationale: The reader first meets a roadmap that was kept in full and did not help, so that the rest arrives as the explanation. The scene names three things the roadmap never stated, and the next three sections supply them in an order each step of which needs the one before: the form of an item comes first because the balance ranks and divides items, and a share of unstated items divides nothing; how far ahead comes third because the horizons vary the form of an item with distance. The horizons section must follow the balance because it ends by joining the two: the share is the commitment that holds across every horizon. What each horizon promises to each audience needs the horizons, and the objection needs that pattern, since it objects to exactly what the pattern withholds; placed earlier, the objection would be answered before the reader knew what was being offered instead of dates. The worked example applies all of it to the opening case, and the AI section is a coda because it asks what happens to the one quantity, the learning cycle, on which the limit rests.

hook.content: In 2024 Corvane's roadmap listed forty-one features, each promised to a large customer by name, each with a date. Corvane shipped all forty-one, thirty-eight of them by the promised date. Its renewal rate fell.

bridge.from_reader_world: A reader who has defended a roadmap to sales, a customer or a board has been asked for features with dates a year out, and has probably given them.
bridge.to_topic: The question is what a roadmap can commit to without becoming false, and how far ahead it can name a solution.

thesis_statement.text: A roadmap should commit to outcomes in an order, with a stated share of capacity for each of innovation, iteration and operation. It can honestly name solutions and dates only as far ahead as one learning cycle of the organization; beyond that it can name only problems, with decreasing precision.

promises.promise: See a roadmap that was delivered in full and failed.

Balance a roadmap across innovation, iteration and operation.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: In 2024 Corvane shipped every one of the forty-one dated features on its roadmap, thirty-eight of them on time and each promised to a named customer, and its renewal rate fell.

evidence.what: Ledger, stage 3 (2024, 180 people): forty-one features in one year, each promised to a named customer, thirty-eight shipped by the promised date; the roadmap a list of features promised to large customers, with dates; the renewal rate fell.
evidence.shows: A roadmap can be kept in full and fail.
evidence.source: _research/scenario-ledger.md (Corvane, fictional)

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A roadmap should commit to outcomes in an order and to a stated share of capacity, and can name solutions and dates only one learning cycle ahead (the time the organization takes to find out whether a solution worked); the chapter goes from Corvane's roadmap, through what a roadmap is for, the balance and the learning cycle with its three horizons, to what each horizon promises, the objection that customers want dates, Corvane's roadmap rewritten, and AI.

transition_in.carries_over: A roadmap kept in full that did not help.
transition_in.introduces: What a roadmap should commit to, and the route through the chapter.

sections.heading: Setting the Scene: A Roadmap Delivered in Full
sections.controlling_idea: Corvane's 2024 roadmap was a list of dated features promised to large customers; it was delivered in full, and it said nothing about outcomes, capacity or how its dates could be known.

advances_thesis.how: Gives the case of a roadmap kept as a delivery contract, whose three faults the following sections take in turn.

transition_in.carries_over: The lead's short account of the forty-one features.
transition_in.introduces: The roadmap itself and how it was made.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Corvane's 2024 roadmap was a list of features, each with the customer it was promised to and a date, added by sales or account management during a deal or a renewal up to a year before delivery.

evidence.what: Illustrative excerpt of the 2024 roadmap, four of forty-one rows: Feature | Promised to | Date. Bulk job import from spreadsheets | a lift-maintenance company | March. Custom billing export format | a heating installer | June. Technician skills matrix | a telecom installer | September. Planner dashboard, version 2 | three large customers | December.
evidence.shows: Shows what a row of the roadmap held: a solution, a requester and a date.
evidence.source: _research/scenario-ledger.md (Corvane, fictional)

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The roadmap was delivered in full and still failed, because nothing on it said what would change for customers, how capacity was divided, or how a date set a year ahead could be known.

evidence.what: All forty-one features shipped in 2024, thirty-eight by the promised date, and the renewal rate fell (ledger).
evidence.shows: Delivery of the list was complete, so the fault is in what the list stated.
evidence.source: _research/scenario-ledger.md (Corvane, fictional)

transition_in.carries_over: A list of promises with dates.
transition_in.introduces: The list kept in full, and the three things it never stated.

sections.heading: What a Roadmap Is For
sections.controlling_idea: A roadmap connects near-term work to the strategy and the vision, so its items are outcomes in an order, and a feature is one candidate solution to an outcome.

advances_thesis.how: Defines the roadmap's job and the form of an item, which the balance and the horizons then act on.

flow.rationale: The roadmap's job comes first, the sales-led version is then recognizable as a departure from it, and the outcome form of an item comes last because it is the remedy to that departure.

transition_in.carries_over: A roadmap that stated solutions and dates only.
transition_in.introduces: What a roadmap is for, and so what an item on it should state.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Build What Matters defines the roadmap's job as connecting near-term product changes to mid-term strategic milestones and the long-term vision so that other teams can plan, which makes its content intended outcomes in an order.

evidence.what: Build What Matters: a roadmap connects the near-term product changes to the mid-term strategic milestones and the long-term vision, helps teams such as marketing and sales plan, and communicates the sequencing of priorities.
evidence.shows: The anchor's definition makes the roadmap a statement of order and direction, not a delivery contract.
evidence.source: Ben Foster and Rajesh Nerlikar, Build What Matters (2020)

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A roadmap assembled from promises to customers is the sales-led roadmap Perri describes, and it is the artifact of the failure pattern this book calls the Feature Factory.

evidence.what: Perri: 'The product roadmap and direction were driven by what was promised to customers, without aligning back to the overall strategy.' She says of sales-led companies that they let their contracts define their product strategy.
evidence.shows: A second source names Corvane's roadmap as a known failure, so it is not a peculiarity of one company.
evidence.source: Melissa Perri, Escaping the Build Trap (2018)

transition_in.carries_over: The roadmap as a connection to strategy and vision.
transition_in.introduces: The roadmap as a list of contracts.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: An item on a roadmap is stated as an outcome, a customer's problem solved to a measured degree, and the feature becomes one candidate solution to it; the problem is what the customer cannot do today, and the outcome adds the measure by which it will count as solved.

evidence.what: As a feature | As an outcome | A measure. Bulk job import from spreadsheets | a new customer's planners schedule their first real week soon after signing | days from signing to the first week scheduled in Corvane. Custom billing export format | a completed job reaches the customer's invoice without anyone retyping it | share of completed jobs invoiced without manual correction. Technician skills matrix | no job is assigned to a technician who is not qualified for it | jobs reassigned for a missing qualification.
evidence.shows: Three of the 2024 features restated, which shows the reader how to do the rewriting and that the outcome leaves the solution open.
evidence.source: _research/scenario-ledger.md (Corvane, fictional)

transition_in.carries_over: A roadmap of features promised by contract.
transition_in.introduces: The form an item takes instead: an outcome with a measure.

sections.heading: Pattern: The Balanced Roadmap
sections.controlling_idea: A roadmap states a share of capacity for each of innovation, iteration and operation, decided before any item is ranked, because without it urgent and customer-specific work takes the whole roadmap.

advances_thesis.how: Supplies the second thing a roadmap commits to, the stated share, from the anchor source.

flow.rationale: The three categories are defined before the rule that allocates among them; the reason for the rule follows it, and the condition under which the share changes comes last because it qualifies a rule the reader must first have.

transition_in.introduces: The second thing the 2024 roadmap never stated: how capacity is divided among kinds of work.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Build What Matters sorts all product development into three categories: innovation, which advances toward the vision; iteration, which improves what exists; and operation, which keeps the product and the business running.

evidence.what: Category | What it is (Build What Matters) | Fed by | At Corvane in 2024. Innovation | progress against strategic milestones toward the vision | vision and strategic planning | nothing on the roadmap. Iteration | better results from what is already built: minor improvements, new features, one-off requests, tests | customer feedback and requests | the skills matrix, the custom export. Operation | maintaining the product and running the business: architecture, performance, security, bug fixes, uptime; 'revenue protection' | bugs, internal tools, technical improvements | the release path that relieved the Launch Queue, which was not on the roadmap.
evidence.shows: Defines the categories in the source's terms and places Corvane's items in them.
evidence.source: Ben Foster and Rajesh Nerlikar, Build What Matters (2020)

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The pattern is to decide the share of capacity for each category top-down before ranking any item, and then to rank items only within their category; it serves the product leader and the executives who agree the split, and it has worked when the share spent each quarter matches the share stated.

evidence.what: Build What Matters recommends starting with a top-down allocation, for example 60 percent to innovation, 30 to iteration and 10 to operation, so that executives understand the trade-offs and big decisions come before small ones. The percentages are the authors' example.
evidence.shows: The allocation rule and its status as an example, not a law.
evidence.source: Ben Foster and Rajesh Nerlikar, Build What Matters (2020)

transition_in.introduces: The rule that divides capacity among them, with its user and measure.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Without a stated share, urgent and customer-specific work takes the whole roadmap, because items of different kinds cannot be compared and the request with the loudest sponsor wins each comparison.

evidence.what: Build What Matters: competing stakeholders with varying influence can have an outsized pull on priorities; a top-down allocation creates space for saying no and spares product managers 'comparing apples to oranges to grapes'.
evidence.shows: The source's reasons for the allocation, which are the mechanism of Corvane's 2024 roadmap.
evidence.source: Ben Foster and Rajesh Nerlikar, Build What Matters (2020)

evidence.what: Corvane 2024: every row had a customer and a date behind it; work on release tooling had neither.
evidence.shows: Shows the mechanism in the opening case.
evidence.source: _research/scenario-ledger.md (Corvane, fictional)

transition_in.introduces: What happens in its absence.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The right share is not fixed: it depends on the product's stage and is revisited, and the operation share in particular is reserved in advance instead of being whatever is left; how the share is set inside budgeting and planning belongs to the planning chapter.

evidence.what: Build What Matters: reserve a percentage of product development for the operation category and rank technical debt, security holes and bugs against each other within it. The author's own record, balanced-roadmap, tunes the split to the product's lifecycle stage.
evidence.shows: States what the share depends on and credits the lifecycle tuning to the author's record.
evidence.source: Ben Foster and Rajesh Nerlikar, Build What Matters (2020); the author's record [[balanced-roadmap]]

transition_in.introduces: What that share depends on.

sections.heading: How Far Ahead: The Learning Cycle and Three Horizons
sections.controlling_idea: A roadmap can name solutions and dates only within one learning cycle of the organization, and beyond it only outcomes and then problems, in three horizons of decreasing precision.

advances_thesis.how: Argues the chapter's specific limit, marks it as the author's position, and turns it into three horizons.

flow.rationale: The asymmetry between solutions and problems is the premise; the learning cycle is the unit the limit is stated in, so it is defined before the limit; the horizons apply the limit and the figure shows items moving through them. The two qualifications come last, since each corrects a wrong conclusion a reader could draw from the limit: that the roadmap should look only one cycle ahead, and that nothing at all can be committed beyond it.

transition_in.carries_over: What a roadmap commits to: outcomes and a share.
transition_in.introduces: The third fault of the 2024 roadmap: how far ahead it named solutions and dates.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: What an organization knows about a solution falls quickly with distance in time, while what it knows about the customer's problem holds.

evidence.what: A solution depends on what the last release taught, on the technology and on what customers do with the current product, all of which change within months; the customer's problem (a planner whose plan breaks when a technician is sick) is the same next year.
evidence.shows: States the asymmetry the limit rests on.

evidence.what: Build What Matters asks, when setting a vision: 'How do we build the right products based on the customer needs that are unlikely to change?' Perri gives four levels of strategy (vision, strategic intent, product initiatives, options), each on a different time horizon.
evidence.shows: Both sources treat needs as the stable part and solutions as the short-lived part, without drawing a limit from it.
evidence.source: Ben Foster and Rajesh Nerlikar, Build What Matters (2020); Melissa Perri, Escaping the Build Trap (2018)

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A learning cycle is the time an organization takes from deciding to try a solution to knowing whether it moved the outcome, and it is the sum of three parts: building and releasing, reaching enough customers, and the measure moving and being read.

evidence.what: Author's definition. Estimated by adding the three parts for a typical roadmap-sized solution; a generic illustration with figures different from Corvane's: four weeks to build and release, two for customers to take it up, two for the measure, about two months.
evidence.shows: Gives the reader the unit and a way to estimate it for their own organization.

transition_in.introduces: The unit in which the decay is measured.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The author's position is that a roadmap can honestly name solutions and dates only within one learning cycle, because a solution named for later is chosen before the result that should choose it exists.

evidence.what: After one cycle the organization knows whether the first solution worked, and that result decides what the next solution should be; a solution written down for the second cycle is decided without it. The sources give the outcome orientation and the balance; neither states this limit.
evidence.shows: The argument for the limit, with its status as the author's position made explicit.

transition_in.introduces: The limit it sets on what a roadmap may name.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The limit gives a roadmap three horizons of decreasing precision: near, where an item is an outcome with a solution and a date; middle, where it is an outcome with a measure and a place in the order; and far, where it is a problem.

evidence.what: Horizon | Reaches | An item states | Example. Near | one learning cycle | the outcome, the solution, a date | 'A customer whose appointment is moved hears it from Corvane first; a message with the new time, released in week 8'. Middle | the next two or three cycles | the outcome, its measure, its place in the order; no solution, no date | 'When a technician is sick, the product proposes a repaired plan and the planner decides; measured by the share of proposals accepted unchanged'. Far | from there to the horizon of the vision | the problem, and roughly where it comes in the order | 'A planner still builds each week's plan by hand'.
evidence.shows: Turns the limit into a form the reader can apply to any roadmap item.

transition_in.introduces: Three horizons that follow from it.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: An item moves from far to near as cycles complete: a problem becomes an outcome with a measure, the outcome gets a solution and a date when it enters the near horizon, and the measured result reorders what waits behind it.

evidence.what: Mermaid flowchart, left to right: 'Far: a problem' → 'Middle: an outcome with a measure' → 'Near: a solution with a date' → 'Result measured'; an edge from 'Result measured' back to 'Middle' labeled 'reorders and restates'; a node 'Vision and strategy' feeding 'Far'.
evidence.shows: Shows the horizons as stages an item passes through, with learning feeding back.

transition_in.introduces: How an item passes through them over time.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The limit shortens what a roadmap promises as solutions and does not shorten how far it looks: Build What Matters names too short a horizon as a dysfunction of its own, the Roller Coaster.

evidence.what: Build What Matters: the Roller Coaster 'comes from setting a time horizon that is too short'; the authors recommend three years as the default horizon for a vision, and reassessing roadmap and vision at one-third or one-quarter of the horizon. These are the authors' rules of thumb.
evidence.shows: Blocks the misreading that an honest roadmap is a one-cycle roadmap.
evidence.source: Ben Foster and Rajesh Nerlikar, Build What Matters (2020)

transition_in.introduces: The opposite error of looking only that far.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The three things on a roadmap are three kinds of statement: the share of capacity is a decision and can be committed a year ahead, the order of outcomes is a judgement that holds until a cycle revises it, and a solution with a date is a prediction that holds for one cycle.

evidence.what: Author's synthesis of the two halves of the chapter: '25 percent to operation this year' is a choice that can be kept whatever the cycles teach; the order of outcomes rests on the strategy and is revised when a result contradicts it; a date for a solution predicts what will have been learned.
evidence.shows: Joins the balance to the horizons and says what can be committed at each distance.

transition_in.carries_over: A roadmap that looks far without naming far solutions.
transition_in.introduces: What it can nevertheless commit to at that distance.

sections.heading: Pattern: One Roadmap with Stated Horizons
sections.controlling_idea: One roadmap, shown to every audience with each horizon labeled by what it promises, gives customers and sales dates in the near horizon and direction beyond it.

advances_thesis.how: Says what the roadmap commits to and to whom, which is the leader's action in the thesis.

transition_in.introduces: What each one promises, and to which audience.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The pattern is to publish one roadmap to every audience with each horizon labeled by what it promises; it serves sales, customers and the board, and it has worked when near-horizon dates are kept and no dated promise exists beyond the near horizon.

evidence.what: Horizon | What is promised | What a customer or salesperson can do with it | What a board can do with it. Near | this solution on this date | plan a rollout, train staff | check delivery against dates. Middle | this outcome, in this order, judged by this measure | know what is coming next and argue about the order | check that the order follows the strategy. Far | this problem is on the list | know the direction of the product | check the direction against the vision.
evidence.shows: Makes 'what a roadmap may promise' specific per horizon and per audience.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Build What Matters warns against letting sales share the internal roadmap, because customers hold the company to it; my recommendation differs in the remedy: a roadmap whose far items are problems can be shown, because it contains no feature to be held to.

evidence.what: Build What Matters: do not let salespeople take the internal roadmap and share it to close deals; once customers have seen it they hold you to it, which removes the flexibility a product manager needs.
evidence.shows: The source's warning, and the point at which the author's recommendation departs from its remedy.
evidence.source: Ben Foster and Rajesh Nerlikar, Build What Matters (2020)

transition_in.introduces: A source that advises keeping the roadmap from customers.

sections.heading: The Objection: Customers and Boards Want Dates
sections.controlling_idea: The demand for dated features a year out rests on a real need to plan, and it is met by what can truthfully be planned on and by a stated way of saying no; a date kept that far ahead is kept by not learning.

advances_thesis.how: Answers the thesis's disputed_by view and gives the trade-offs among honest answers to a demand for a date.

transition_in.carries_over: A roadmap that gives direction beyond the near horizon.
transition_in.introduces: The view that this is evasion.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The objection from sales, customers and boards is that a roadmap is a commitment to deliver named features on dates and that anything less is evasion, and the need behind it is real: they have plans of their own that depend on the product.

evidence.what: A customer signing a multi-year contract, a salesperson closing a deal and a board approving a budget each have to plan on something.
evidence.shows: States the opposing view at its strongest.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A date for a named feature beyond the learning cycle can be kept only by fixing the solution before the evidence arrives, as Corvane did; what the objectors need is something true to plan on, and the order, the share, the near dates and the record of dates kept are that.

evidence.what: Corvane shipped all forty-one promised features in 2024, thirty-eight on the promised date, and its renewal rate fell.
evidence.shows: A kept date is not evidence that the promise was worth making.
evidence.source: _research/scenario-ledger.md (Corvane, fictional)

transition_in.introduces: Why a far date does not meet it, and what does.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: When a date beyond the near horizon is still demanded there are three honest answers, and which is right depends on where the date comes from: direction only, a fixed date with open scope, or a dated feature as a priced exception.

evidence.what: Answer | What is given | Right when | Cost. Direction only | the outcome and its place in the order | the date is a wish | some deals are harder to close. Fixed date, open scope | the date, and the outcome to be reached by it; the solution stays open | the date is set by the world: a regulation, a contract end, a customer's own launch | scope is cut to keep the date. Priced exception | a named feature on a date | one customer's need justifies it and someone senior spends limited capacity on it | capacity leaves the iteration share, visibly.
evidence.shows: Gives the trade-off table the style guide asks for, with the condition for each choice.

evidence.what: Build What Matters recounts a company that gave the head of sales a limited number of tokens for one-off requests, after which most such requests stopped reaching product management.
evidence.shows: A published account of pricing exceptions; presented as that book's anecdote.
evidence.source: Ben Foster and Rajesh Nerlikar, Build What Matters (2020)

transition_in.carries_over: What can truthfully be planned on.
transition_in.introduces: The cases where a date is demanded anyway.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Most requests are not demands for a date, and a roadmap with a stated share and stated horizons gives the general way of answering them: a request is recorded, competes inside the iteration share, and is declined with the reason when it does not make it.

evidence.what: Build What Matters: a hallmark of product-driven companies is being able to say no; keep an idea bank for suggestions not on the roadmap, and be transparent about what did not make it and why; product managers who cannot say no end up playing 'product management Tetris'.
evidence.shows: The source's practice for refusing, which the share and the horizons make possible.
evidence.source: Ben Foster and Rajesh Nerlikar, Build What Matters (2020)

transition_in.introduces: The general answer to any request for something not on the roadmap.

sections.heading: Worked Example: Corvane's Roadmap, Rewritten
sections.controlling_idea: Rewritten in mid-2025 with a stated share and three horizons, Corvane's roadmap named solutions and dates for one quarter only, and the first cycle's result chose a second solution that no list written in advance could have named.

advances_thesis.how: Applies the balance, the learning cycle and the horizons to the opening case and shows the limit doing its work.

flow.rationale: The steps are given in the order Priya Nambiar took them: classify what had been shipped, estimate the cycle, write the roadmap, read the first result. The roadmap table precedes any judgement of it, and the costs come last so that the result is not read as a clean success.

transition_in.introduces: The patterns applied to the roadmap the chapter opened with.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: In mid-2025 Priya Nambiar, Corvane's new CPO, first classified the 2024 roadmap: all forty-one rows were iteration, none was innovation, and operation work was not on the roadmap at all.

evidence.what: Illustration: mid-2025, Corvane growing toward 500 people. Every one of the forty-one rows of 2024 was a customer request (iteration in the Build What Matters sense); no row advanced toward a vision; the release path that relieved the Launch Queue in 2024 was operation work and appeared on no roadmap.
evidence.shows: Shows the balance of the old roadmap, which nobody had chosen.
evidence.source: _research/scenario-ledger.md (Corvane, fictional)

paragraphs.controlling_idea: She then estimated Corvane's learning cycle at about a quarter: six weeks to build and release a roadmap-sized solution, three for customers to switch it on, four for the measure to move and be read.

evidence.what: Illustration: 6 + 3 + 4 = 13 weeks, with a median lead time for a single change under 7 days.
evidence.shows: Applies the three-part estimate and fixes Corvane's near horizon at one quarter.
evidence.source: _research/scenario-ledger.md (Corvane, fictional)

transition_in.carries_over: The balance of the old roadmap.
transition_in.introduces: The length of the near horizon for the new one.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The roadmap of mid-2025 stated a share of 40 percent innovation, 35 iteration and 25 operation, and laid seven items over three horizons, following the order of Corvane's strategy.

evidence.what: Horizon | Category | The item as stated | What Corvane promises. Near (third quarter of 2025) | Innovation | a customer whose appointment is moved hears it from Corvane before calling the office; a message with the new time and a link to accept it or ask for another, released in week 8; measure: share of appointment changes that reach the customer first, about a third today, target two thirds by the end of the cycle | the solution and the date. Near | Iteration | the features written into customer contracts in 2024 whose contract dates fall in this quarter | the solution and the date, promised by contract before the roadmap changed. Near | Operation | a completed job reaches the customer's billing system the same day; the nightly export's retry rebuilt, week 5 | the solution and the date. Middle (to mid-2026) | Innovation | when a technician is sick, the product proposes a repaired plan and the planner decides; measure: share of proposals accepted unchanged | the outcome and its place in the order. Middle | Iteration | planners stop keeping a second schedule in a spreadsheet; measure: share of planners who still keep one | the outcome and its place in the order. Far (to 2028) | Innovation | a planner still builds each week's plan by hand | direction. Far | Operation | each large customer's billing and stock integration is built separately | direction.

sections.heading: What AI Changes Here
sections.controlling_idea: AI shortens the building part of the learning cycle, so the near horizon may cover less calendar time while more is learned in it, and it also makes the dated feature list cheaper to keep.

transition_in.introduces: Whether that length holds when agents do part of the building.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Emerging: coding agents shorten the building part of the learning cycle, and building is only one of its three parts, so the cycle shortens by less than the building does.

evidence.what: Author's observation as of November 2026, labeled Emerging and not measured: teams using coding agents produce a first version of a solution in less time; customers' take-up and the measure's movement are customers' time and do not shorten with it.
evidence.shows: Gives the label and its basis, and limits the claim to one part of the cycle.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Speculative: if the learning cycle shortens, the near horizon covers less calendar time, more cycles fit in a year, and more is learned inside each stretch of the roadmap, so less of a year's roadmap can be stated as solutions and its outcomes are reached, or dropped, sooner.

evidence.what: Labeled Speculative; follows from the limit of this chapter. It would be confirmed where organizations report more solution attempts per outcome per quarter and shorter dated portions of their roadmaps.
evidence.shows: States what follows for horizons and what would confirm it.

transition_in.introduces: What a shorter cycle does to the horizons.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Speculative: cheaper building also makes the dated feature list cheaper to keep, so the Feature Factory becomes more tempting, not less.

evidence.what: Labeled Speculative; when a requested feature costs days, building it looks cheaper than refusing it. It would be confirmed where organizations with agents ship more customer-requested features per quarter with no change in their outcome measures.

conclusion.heading: What to Take Away
conclusion.synthesis: The two halves of the chapter are one rule about what kind of statement each part of a roadmap is: a share is a decision and can be committed for a year, an order of outcomes is a judgement that holds until a cycle revises it, and a solution with a date is a prediction that holds for one cycle.
conclusion.so_what: The reader can publish one roadmap that customers, sales and a board can plan on, defend the capacity for operation and iteration with a number, and decline a far date with a reason.

callback.to: Corvane's forty-one dated features, all shipped, with a falling renewal rate.
callback.how: The reader can now say what that roadmap committed to (solutions and dates a year out, with no outcome and no stated share) and what it should have committed to.

takeaway.content: Take your current roadmap, estimate your learning cycle, and restate every item beyond it as an outcome or a problem. The checklist that follows gives the steps.
